content:
Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body, along with extreme tiredness, poor sleep and problems with memory and concentration, often called "fibro fog". It does not damage joints, and it is not arthritis, though the two can occur together. There is no cure, but exercise, pacing, psychological support and some medicines can help people live well.

Symptoms

  • widespread pain that may feel aching, burning or stabbing
  • increased sensitivity to pain, touch, temperature, noise or bright lights
  • fatigue that is not relieved by rest
  • unrefreshing sleep
  • stiffness
  • fibro fog: problems with memory, concentration and finding words
  • headaches, irritable bowel symptoms and low mood

Symptoms often vary from day to day, with flare-ups triggered by stress, illness, poor sleep or overdoing things.

What causes it

The exact cause is not fully understood. Fibromyalgia is thought to involve changes in how the brain and nerves process pain signals, sometimes called central sensitisation. It often starts after a physical or emotional trigger, such as an injury, infection, surgery or a stressful life event. It is more common in women and can run in families. It is also more common in people with rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and other conditions.

Getting diagnosed

There is no blood test or scan for fibromyalgia. Your GP will ask about your symptoms and may arrange tests to rule out other conditions with similar features, such as an underactive thyroid, vitamin D deficiency, polymyalgia rheumatica or inflammatory arthritis. Diagnosis is based on widespread pain lasting at least three months along with other typical symptoms.

Treatment: what NICE recommends

NICE's chronic pain guideline (NG193) covers fibromyalgia as a type of chronic primary pain. It recommends:

  • exercise programmes tailored to the person, built up gradually
  • psychological therapies such as CBT or acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), to help manage the impact of pain
  • acupuncture, as a single course in some cases
  • an antidepressant may be considered for some people, even if they do not have depression, because some help with pain and sleep

NICE advises against starting many commonly used painkillers for chronic primary pain, including opioids, paracetamol, NSAIDs and gabapentinoids, because the harms are likely to outweigh the benefits. If you already take these, do not stop suddenly. Talk to your GP about a review.

Self-help that makes a difference

  • Start exercise low and slow. Walking, swimming, gentle cycling or tai chi. Increase by small amounts. A short walk most days is better than a long one once a week.
  • Pace yourself. Plan activity and rest so that you do not have big boom-and-bust cycles.
  • Sleep routine. Go to bed and wake at the same time, limit caffeine and screens in the evening.
  • Manage stress. Relaxation, mindfulness or breathing exercises can calm the nervous system.
  • Stay connected. Support groups and talking to friends reduce isolation.

Work and money

You may be entitled to reasonable adjustments at work under the Equality Act 2010. Benefits such as PIP depend on how fibromyalgia affects your daily life rather than the diagnosis itself.

Living well

Fibromyalgia does not shorten life or cause joint damage. Many people find their symptoms improve over time with the right mix of activity, pacing and support. If your symptoms change, such as new swollen joints, weight loss or fevers, see your GP, as these are not typical of fibromyalgia.

Talking to others about fibromyalgia

Because fibromyalgia is invisible, people around you may not understand how it affects you. Explaining that it is a recognised long-term condition, and that energy and pain vary day to day, can help. Some people find it useful to share NHS information with family or their employer. Peer support groups, in person or online, can also offer practical tips and reassurance.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
